source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Early GPT-3 models answer Cognitive Reflection Test items with the intuitive wrong answer, like humans. ChatGPT and GPT-4 mostly stop doing so.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks. Intuitive answers: GPT-3-davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. Correct: davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%.
limits: Task items are generated by the authors, not the original three CRT items. Human data comes from a prior study (n=3,428). Training-set contamination cannot be excluded.
agent_relevance: The fast-wrong pattern of humans is model-dependent. A strong model needs less forced slowing; do not assume human System 1 errors for every model.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Step-by-step instruction rescues the weaker model on CRT: intuitive answers fall and correct answers rise.
numbers: davinci-003 with step-by-step instruction: correct 5% to 28%; intuitive 80% to 29%; share of chain-of-thought responses 0% to 100%.
limits: Only the older GPT-3 model was tested here. 29% intuitive errors remain.
agent_relevance: Writing steps is a cheap slow-mode switch for weak models. The gain is partial.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Forbidding chain-of-thought in ChatGPT barely hurts CRT accuracy. The newer models have an intuition that already beats the traps without visible steps.
numbers: Forced no-reasoning: ChatGPT-3.5 chain-of-thought share 97% to 0%, correct change not significant (4 points, p=.49). ChatGPT-4 chain-of-thought 84% to 0%; correct 95% to 88%; intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: Small drop only for ChatGPT-4. CRT-style math traps only.
agent_relevance: For strong models, fast single-shot output is not the same as human System 1. Fast mode may be enough on trap-type problems.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: A handful of solved examples teaches the model to avoid CRT traps without reasoning steps.
numbers: davinci-003, 0 to 49 solved examples. CRT type 2: 2% to 92% after two examples. Type 3: 12% to 92% after seven. Type 1: 0% to about 78% after 30.
limits: Examples and tests are the same task type. Transfer to new trap types is not shown.
agent_relevance: Matches the expertise view: repeated worked cases make the fast route correct. Supports retrieving worked cases for S0.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Semantic illusions (questions with a hidden false assumption) follow the same shape as CRT: GPT-3 falls for them, ChatGPT-4 mostly catches them.
numbers: Fell for illusion: davinci-003 72%. Correct: davinci-003 18%, ChatGPT-3.5 74%, ChatGPT-4 88%. Humans: 52% intuitive in the original study (n=61), 64% in the authors' sample.
limits: Human comparison data are small and from a different study.
agent_relevance: Detecting invalid premises is within fast pattern recognition for strong models; slow mode is not needed for it.

source: Binz, Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci) gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three CRT items and fell for the Linda conjunction fallacy, but not the cab base-rate problem.
numbers: 12 vignettes: 6 answered correctly, all 12 answers human-like. CRT: 3 of 3 intuitive. Linda: conjunction error. Cab problem: approximately correct.
limits: Famous vignettes are probably in the training data. Temperature 0, one model.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that LLM fast mode copies human System 1 errors on classic tasks.

source: Binz, Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: Small surface changes to vignettes break GPT-3. Success on classic tasks may be memory, not analysis.
numbers: Black-cab variant: answered 20% although 15% blue, 85% green. Wason with reordered cards (4,7,A,K): chose A and K. CRT with the text 'bat costs $1.00 more than the bat': still answered $0.10.
limits: Anecdotal adversarial variants, no sample sizes.
agent_relevance: The agent should check answers on mutated problems (G3). Retrieving a famous pattern can look like analysis.

source: Binz, Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: The same model that fails the CRT shows deliberate model-based behaviour in a two-step reinforcement task, so fast and slow are task-specific, not model-wide.
numbers: Two-step task: 200 simulations of 20 repetitions; stay probability fell after a rare rewarded transition t(1982)=-6.16, p<.001; rose after a rare unrewarded one t(1814)=2.33, p=.01.
limits: Statistical signature only. It is not proof of internal planning.
agent_relevance: A model has no single dual-process setting. Mode choice must be made per task, driven by checks.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic Reasoning Prompts Reveal the Potential for Large Language Model Interpretability in Medicine
finding: Prompting GPT-4 to reason in a named clinical style (intuitive, analytic, differential, Bayesian) on USMLE diagnosis questions did not change accuracy much versus plain chain-of-thought.
numbers: MedQA Step 2/3 diagnosis, 518 test questions (95 for prompt tuning). GPT-4: plain CoT 76%, intuitive 77% (+0.8, p=.73), differential 78% (+2.2, p=.24), analytic 78% (+1.6, p=.35), Bayesian 72% (-3.4, p=.07).
limits: Multiple-choice exam items, not real patients. Two-shot prompts. No difference is not proof of equivalence.
agent_relevance: Naming a reasoning mode is a weak lever for a strong model. Matches the human finding that 'use System 2' instructions do little.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic Reasoning Prompts Reveal the Potential for Large Language Model Interpretability in Medicine
finding: For weaker GPT-3.5, forced analytic, differential or Bayesian styles hurt; the intuitive style matched plain chain-of-thought.
numbers: GPT-3.5: plain CoT 46%; intuitive 48% (p=0.9); analytic 40% (-6, p=.001); differential 38% (-8, p<.001); Bayesian 42% (-4, p=.02). Rater agreement 97%, kappa .93.
limits: Same prompts for both models.
agent_relevance: Slow-style prompts can backfire on weak models. Mode forcing needs a capability check.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks
finding: SwiftSage is an LLM agent built on dual-process theory: a small fine-tuned model acts fast (Swift); GPT-4 plans and corrects only when needed (Sage). Rules in code, not the model, decide the switch.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types. Mean score: SwiftSage 84.7, Reflexion 45.3, ReAct 36.4, SayCan 33.8, DRRN 11.4.
limits: Needs oracle trajectories to train Swift. One benchmark. Reflexion had up to four rounds, others one.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S0: code-triggered handover from fast to slow mode.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks
finding: The Swift to Sage switch is rule-based and fires on four conditions.
numbers: Switch to Sage when: five consecutive steps with zero reward; the predicted action is invalid; a critical decision such as the final answer; or an exception is suggested. Return to Swift after Sage's actions run.
limits: Thresholds (five steps) are hand-set.
agent_relevance: This is the 'doubt only on a signal' rule (G1) in working form. We can copy the four kinds of signal.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks
finding: The dual design costs fewer tokens than slow-only agents.
numbers: Tokens per action: SayCan 1,855.84, ReAct 1,971.03, Reflexion 2,983.46, SwiftSage 757.07.
limits: Swift is fine-tuned, so training cost is outside this count.
agent_relevance: A fast default with rare slow calls cut token cost by about 60 to 75 percent in this setup.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Forced step-by-step thinking lowers accuracy on tasks where deliberation also hurts people: implicit statistical learning, face recognition, classification with exceptions.
numbers: Implicit learning: o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o 94.0% zero-shot (36.3 points lower, p<.0001; subset). Face recognition zero-shot to CoT: GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2; Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6; Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0 to 54.6. Exceptions: GPT-4o iterations to learn 2.9 to 12.5 (+331%).
limits: Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed no drop on some tasks (e.g. 65.9 to 67.7 on one). Three task families only; not every human-poor-thinking task transferred.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that 'always slow' is wrong. The S0 mode choice must be able to pick fast.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus 20 datasets and 14 models: chain-of-thought helps mostly on math, logic and symbolic tasks, little elsewhere.
numbers: Up to 95% of CoT's gain on MMLU comes from questions with an equals sign in the question or output. Gains in commonsense, knowledge and soft-reasoning categories are mostly not significant.
limits: Prompt-based CoT only; a symbolic solver beat CoT on the symbolic tasks.
agent_relevance: Use the slow route where a symbolic or checkable step exists. For recall-style diagnosis items, spend little on it.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models spend large compute on trivial questions, and extra solution rounds add little accuracy.
numbers: For 'what is the answer of 2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one example gave 13 solutions. A self-training fix cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview at the same accuracy.
limits: Math benchmarks only (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME).
agent_relevance: The cost of the wrong mode is measurable. Slow mode on easy items is waste; supports a cheap fast first pass.

source: Weston, Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: System 2 Attention: the model rewrites the input to keep only relevant parts, then answers. It removes opinion and irrelevant context that sway fast answers.
numbers: Opinionated factual QA (LLaMA-2-70B-chat): baseline 62.8%, oracle unopinionated 82.0%, S2A 80.3%. Math with distractor sentences: 51.7% to 61.3%.
limits: Costs an extra generation. One model family, GPT-4 grading.
agent_relevance: A reframe-then-answer step guards against anchoring on leading or irrelevant input, like clinician anchoring. Candidate operator.

source: Yu, Xu, Weston, Kulikov (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Slow-method outputs can be trained back into fast answers, like automatisation in human expertise.
numbers: Last-letter task (Llama-2-70B-chat): zero-shot 30.0%, 2-step Rephrase-and-Respond 44.5%, distilled 98.0% with 25.5 tokens vs 106.6. SycophancyEval biased inputs: zero-shot 51.6%, S2A 76.0%, distilled S2A 81.3% at 56 tokens vs 147. Without consistency filtering 78.6%.
limits: Needs training data and fine-tuning; outside our no-training scope.
agent_relevance: Slow tools can pay back as compiled fast rules. Fits a reusable case library.

source: Kojima et al. (2022) Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
finding: Adding 'Let's think step by step' is a one-line slow-mode switch with large gains on arithmetic.
numbers: InstructGPT large model: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%; GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7%.
limits: Gains are on symbolic tasks; Sprague (2025) shows small gains elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Baseline slow-mode lever. Cheap but task-limited.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Cognitive-bias cues planted in USMLE questions lower accuracy in every model tested. This is the machine version of anchoring and availability errors.
numbers: 1,273 USMLE questions, seven biases. No-bias accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7B 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4%. GPT-4 with false-consensus cue 62.5%, recency 67.9%. Average drop by bias: false consensus 24.9, frequency 18.2, recency 12.9, confirmation 8.1 points.
limits: Table layout was garbled in text extraction; only cells confirmed by the prose are cited.
agent_relevance: Leading wording in a case biases the model. Strip suggestions from the problem restatement.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: A short 'beware of bias' warning helps GPT-4 partly; bias examples help more; weaker models gain little.
numbers: GPT-4 false consensus: 62.5% baseline, 68.7% with education text, 74.5% few-shot (no-bias 72.7%). Frequency bias 62.7% to 72.0% with education. PaLM-2 refused 94.4% of one-shot and 99.5% of few-shot queries.
limits: GPT-4 benefit is not seen in the other models. One benchmark built by inserting cue text.
agent_relevance: Parallels human cognitive-forcing results: awareness alone is weak, worked examples are better.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: LLMs show framing, group-attribution and primacy patterns in student-admission decisions. Prompt-level debiasing helps; example-based debiasing can break instruction following.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Llama-2-7B labelled 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Few-shot and counterfactual mitigation sometimes drove admit or reject rate to 0 or 1. Having the model rewrite its own prompt ('self-help') gave better primacy results than awareness text.
limits: Not a medical task. Numbers are shifts in admission rate, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Having the model rewrite its own prompt to remove bias works like a reframe step.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: A reasoning model (o1-preview, trained for long chain-of-thought) beat physicians and GPT-4 on differential diagnosis and reasoning documentation.
numbers: 143 NEJM cases: correct dx in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7 to 84.8); first suggestion correct 52%. Exact or close dx 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9%. Reasoning score median 86% vs GPT-4 42%, physicians with GPT-4 41%, physicians alone 34%. Real emergency cases: 65.8% at triage vs physicians 54.4% and 48.1%.
limits: Text-only cases; no real-time use; some physician controls historical. Management-reasoning score was similar to GPT-4 (p=0.7).
agent_relevance: A trained slow mode helps diagnosis, yet the first guess is right only about half the time.

source: Xie et al. (2024) A Preliminary Study of o1 in Medicine: Are We Closer to an AI Doctor?
finding: o1 beats GPT-4 on medical tasks on average. Extra chain-of-thought still helps o1 a little; heavier methods hurt.
numbers: o1 over GPT-4 by an average 6.2% across 19 datasets. CoT prompt added 3.18% to o1's 83.6% on knowledge QA. Self-consistency and reflexion lowered accuracy by 12.8% on average versus CoT on LancetQA. Hallucination remained.
limits: Benchmark exams; prompts not tuned.
agent_relevance: Stacking more slow steps on an already slow model can hurt. Keep slow tools few.

source: Huang et al. (2025) m1: Unleash the Potential of Test-Time Scaling for Medical Reasoning with LLMs
finding: In medical reasoning, more thinking helps up to about 4K tokens, then accuracy falls. Knowledge, not reasoning depth, is the bottleneck.
numbers: Optimal reasoning budget about 4K tokens; beyond it accuracy declines (overthinking). Fine-tuned 7B models set new best results under 10B; the 32B model is comparable to 70B medical models.
limits: Fine-tuned open models; benchmark questions.
agent_relevance: Cap slow-mode budget. Add knowledge (retrieved cases or guidelines) rather than more steps.

source: Booch et al. (2020) Thinking Fast and Slow in AI
finding: Position paper proposing an AI with a fast System 1 solver, a slow System 2 solver and a metacognitive module that picks between them. No experiments.
numbers: None reported; research questions only.
limits: Proposal only. Later work built on it was not opened here.
agent_relevance: Supports a separate mode-choice module, which in our schema is code (S0).

source: Christakopoulou et al. (2024) Agents Thinking Fast and Slow: A Talker-Reasoner Architecture
finding: Two-agent LLM design: a fast Talker talks to the user using stored beliefs; a slow Reasoner plans and updates beliefs in the background. A flag lets the Talker wait for the Reasoner.
numbers: Case study of a sleep-coaching agent. No accuracy numbers reported.
limits: Demonstration only. The authors admit the Talker works from out-of-date beliefs.
agent_relevance: Shows a fast/slow split in an agent loop but no measured gain. Do not cite it as evidence of benefit.
